text:
(informative)

                         Accessible and inclusive cybersecurity

This annex facuses on enabling manufacturers of consumer cyber products to produce products which
are both secure and accessible to the users.
title: Scope

text:
The EuropeanAccessibility Act (EAA) UQ]_ requires thata wide range of products and services, including
smartphones, ATMs, e-commerce platfarms, and e-readers, are usable by persons with disabilities. This
aligns with the EU's commitment to equal participation in society and the economy, ensuring that no
consumer is excluded from the digitai marketplace.
Security features are often the "front door" to a digitai product. If a consumer cannot navigate
authentication, password recovery, or consent dialogues, they can be left vulnerable-or unable to use
the product at ali. Accessibility in cybersecurity is therefare both a compliance issue under the EAA and
a trust issue far manufacturers who want to serve the widest possible market.
At the same time, the CRA li places obligations on manufacturers to safeguard the users' cybersecurity.
Devices and digitai services are increasingly interconnected, and secure design is essential to protect
consumers from fraud, identity theft, and misuse of persona} data. Therefare it is important that,_
cybersecurity measures themselves are accessible-otherwise they can inadvertently exclude or
disadvantage certain groups of users.
Accessibility and cybersecurity are two sides of the same coin: both protect users, both reduce exclusion,
and both are essential far building a sustainable digitai economy.
title: Legai reasoning

text:
Cybersecurity is often designed with the "ideai user" in mind. This ideai user has a limitless memory
and attention to detail, to enable them to be fully aware of system behaviours that indicate suspect
behaviours and the ability to retain and apply ali the rules in organization policies. Very few humans
have ali these abiliti es ali of the time. This is why it is crucial to create a good understanding of what
can be reasonably expected ofthe user demographics, as otherwise many potential users will struggle
and may fail to use the product safely.
When developing cybersecurity solutions, it is required to consider the user abilities and skills needed
to carry out the required interactions with the product. Consumers will be impacted depending on:
      The nature ofthe required interaction.
      The consequence ofthe interaction method on the user's cybersecurity.
      The recommended solution to ensure maximum cybersecurity to the potential users.
Limiting the types of users who can interact with a product will harm people with disabilities and also
people with temporary conditions caused by accident, illness, stress, grief or distraction.




                                                                                                        53

prEN 40000-1-2 (E)
title: Theuser

text:
The nature of the required interaction can include (but is not limited to) the following:
      interactions requiring the use of visual or audible information can reduce the cybersecurity for
      blind/visually impaired/colour-blind and/or deaf/hard of hearing people.
      interactions requiring the operation of physical controls can reduce the cybersecurity for people
      with gross or fine control motor control issues, reach issues and/or related issues.
      interactions requiring the understanding of spoken or written information can reduce the
      cybersecurity for people who cannot read or understand a particular language or who have a
      cognitive disability.
      interactions requiring speech control can reduce the cybersecurity for people who are speech
      impaired.
title: Nature of the required interaction

text:
Examples of accessibility issues in cybersecurity requirements include systems which require people
to have specific physical, visual, hearing, memory or cognitive skills. Examples of these are presented
with possible solutions below:
      Systems that time-out too quickly during password entry can disadvantage users who rely on
      assistive technologies such as screen readers or switch devices. Extending the time-out will also
      benefit other users includingthose with physical disabilities or whose attention is limited by stress.
      Biometrie authentication, as facial recognition can fail for users with certain physical disabilities
      or conditions that affect their appearance or ability to stay stili or who are using a system without
      a camera (or fingerprint sensor). Offering multiple authentication methods will enable more
      consumers to authenticate themselves. Ali single method verification methods can cause issues:
           SMS-based codes can be inaccessible to people with hearing loss if voice cali verification is the
           only backup.
           CAPTCHA challenges relying on distorted text or images exclude users with visual loss unless
           multiple, accessible, alternatives (e.g., audio CAPTCHAs or logical puzzles) are provided.
           Fingerprint scanners cannot be usable by individuals with prosthetics or reduced dexterity
           or whose fingerprints are not easily readable due to skin changes caused by age.
           Pop-up alerts that disappear quickly can be inaccessible to users relying on screen readers or
           whose reaction times are reduced by physical factors (temporary by accident or long-term
           physical functional limitation or by slow reactions (caused by stress or cognitive issues or
           distraction by children etc.).
      Cybersecurity updates or recovery processes that depend on a single method of delivery and also
      use unclear terminology will be inaccessible to a range of users.
title: Consequences of the interaction method on the user's cybersecurity

text:
potential users
For each interaction, suitable alternatives can be identified using different skills and abilities. Providing
alternative methods of interacting with the product and with communicating to the user information
about the product will enable more users to interact with the product. These changes will not impact
the cybersecurity of the product. User stories can be a valuable input in considering what alternatives
to provide to ensure accessibility to the product.



54

                                                                                   prEN 40000-1-2 (E)



Accessibility requirements and advice can be found in EN 301 549 v3.2.1 "Accessibility requirements
for ICT products and services". Accounting forthese requirements is better done earlier in development
as adding accessibility features can also potentially add vulnerabilities and as such these need to be
accounted for in the risk assessment.


D. 7   Communication with the user
The obligation of the manufacturer to provi de accessibility to the design of the product also extends to
the accessibility of the communication with the user. This is to ensure the user is capable of accessing
the information required for securely installing, operating, maintaining and decommissioning the
product. By conducting heuristic evaluation, cognitive walkthroughs, and accessibilitytesting alongside
cybersecurity testing and design analysis, providing alternative methods of se cure access, and ensuring
compatibility with assistive technologies, manufacturers can not only reduce regulatory risk but also
strengthen consumer trust.

Introduction
Vulnerabilities are likely to emerge aver time during the life cycle of a product with digitai elements
(hereinafter referred to as "product"), including its software and hardware components, despite
adherence to cybersecurity principles defined in prEN 40000-1-2 [1].
It is important to prepare far those events by developing an effective strategy far the management of
vulnerabilities during the product life cycle, including regular monitoring, testing, risk assessment,
prioritization, remediation, and verification, as well as communication, which are all essential activities
to discover and fix new vulnerabilities and maintain cybersecurity coverage.
This vulnerability handling document refines the activities that are part of international standards such
as EN ISO/IEC 30111:2020 [21. EN ISO/IEC 29147:2020 [31 and ISO/IEC TR 5895:2022 [4]. It elevates,
where appropriate, recommendations to manda tory requirements to ensure confarmity with the Cyber
Resilience Act (CRA) obligations. It integrates essential elements such as Software Bill of Materials
(SBOM), regular testing and review activities, secure update mechanisms, and explicit requirements to
support effective Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure (CVD) and vulnerability-handling processes.
The rigar with which vulnerability handling activities are expected to be executed are expected to adhere
to a risk-based approach, determined by the potential societal impact of a product's security failure.
Far example, the regular test and other monitoring activities are expected to be executed more
frequently far products with higher criticality, and having a more detailed SBOM can improve the
detection of vulnerabilities in components used by the product. The horizontal standards far the Cyber
Resilience Act cannot be tao prescriptive and thus require appropriate product risk-based criteria to
be documented in the risk assessment and the cybersecurity pian far the product.

The vulnerability handling activities defined in this documentare organized into the following distinct
phases:
    Preparation: Establishing policies, processes, and capabilities for vulnerability intake and
    disclosure.
    Receipt: Receiving and monito ring vulnerability reports from internal and external sources.
    Verification: Assessing the validity, applicability, and severity of reported vulnerabilities.
    Remediation: Planning, developing, and testing fixes or mitigations.
    Release: Distributing security updates and publishing advisories.
    Post-Release: Monitoring effectiveness and applying lessons learned.
Manufacturers implementing this document will be equipped to demonstrate due diligence in
vulnerability handling, maintain product security over time, and support transparency and trust across
the digitai ecosystem.

5.3.3     [PRE-2] Policy on coordinated vulnerability disclosure



12

title: Assessment criteria

text:
The purpose of the coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy is to communicate the manufacturer's
intentions, responsibilities, and expectations regarding vulnerability disclosure. A coordinated
vulnerability disclosure policy encompasses both two-party coordinati on (e.g. between the reporter
and the manufacturer) and multi-party disclosure involving multiple stakeholders. To support this, the
manufacturer develops and publishes an external coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy and
ensures the related internal activities are in piace to effectively coordinate the disclosure of
vulnerabilities.
In addition, to prevent attackers from gaining early access to sensitive information, reporters typically
notify manufacturers privately, and refrain from public disclosure until a fix is available after an agreed-
upon embargo period has passed. The receipt, verification, and remediation development stages are
generally conducted within this embargo period, ensuring that vulnerabilities are addressed securely
and responsibly by ali the parties involved in the process.

5.4.8     [RCP-7] Performing regolar reviews
title: Assessment criteria

text:
Maintaining a product's security is an ongoing task. This includes performing security tests throughout
the product's support period. It also includes activities to reassess the threats and risks posed to the
product due to changes in cybersecurity attack techniques or the way the product is used in practical
conditions.
The needs regarding these regular tests and reviews depend on the type of product and its use. A simple
product developed on demand fora specific customer and purpose, as an individuai unit, might require
very few actions, while a more complex product supplied in large quantities for exposure to the Internet
might require stringent monitoring.
The security risk a product is exposed to is not static. It changes as attack methods or the threat landscape
evolves. This can, for example, include knowledge of cryptographic algorithms' strengths.
It can also turn out that the product context is not correctly described. For example, the product's use
or operational environment may differ from the description during practical use.

5.5     [VRF] Verification

reported vulnerability affects the product. lt also includes requirements for prioritizing the vulnerability
based on vulnerability risk assessment activities.
The primary objective of this phase is to assess the validity, reproducibility, and applicability of the
reported vulnerability. During this phase, the received information is reviewed to determine whether
it is complete and whether the vulnerability is genuine and applicable to the product in question. Ifa
vulnerability is assessed as relevant, the security risk analysis is performed to determine whether the
risk associated with the vulnerability is to be mitigated and, if so, with what priority.

5895:2022 [41 . 9.2.

separated, all the activities listed can occur in parallel rather than in a sequential order.

5. 7.2     [RLS-1] Security update release

5. 7.2.1    Generai
This subclause addresses the activities of gathering ali the artefacts to address vulnerabilities and
disseminating security updates.
Any delay in applying security updates gives attackers time to exploit the product's vulnerabilities.
Therefare, the timely distribution of security updates is essential. A secure update distribution
mechanism ensures the integrity and authenticity of security updates. An automatic update distribution
mechanism ensures that vulnerabilities are remediated without user interaction far the products that
support automatic updates.
Such updates need to be provided in a secure manner, which might, far example, use digitai signatures
and/ or secure download services.
Security updates are to be applied automatically or manually depending on the type of product, its

Introduction

Machinery must be safe in order to prevent injuries and loss of life.
The communication with the machine must not lead to hazardous situations.
The manufacturer performs a risk assessment according to EN ISO 12100 to identify all potential hazards.
Vulnerabilities can lead to a corruption of the control system of the machine and hazards can lead to dangerous
situations.
By exploitation of vulnerabilities via communication with the machine, the machine could be operated outside
safe parameters or degrade safety functions.
Vulnerabilities cannot create new hazards.
The probability that someone will use a vulnerability for a malicious attempt cannot be predicted.
The risk can only be assessed in terms of its impact on functional safety.
Vulnerabilities are divided into several types.
This document provides two approaches:
—   Approach A (Clause 5 and 7) has been developed to facilitate compliance for machinery developed without
references to EN IEC 62443 series of standards.

—   Approach B (Clauses 6 and 8) has been provided to facilitate compliance for machinery developed in the
context of the EN IEC 62443-3-3:2019, EN IEC 62443-4-1:2018, EN IEC 62443-4-2:2019.

NOTE 1     The EN IEC 62443 series provides information and a methodology to approach cybersecurity.

This document is intended for use by machinery designers, control system manufacturers and integrators, and
others involved in the specification, design and validation of an SCS.
NOTE 2     See EN IEC 62443-4-1:2018; the manufacturer can be a product supplier or system integrator.

This document does not address the role of the user.

1   Scope

This document provides requirements and recommendations for protection against corruption for machinery,
related products and partly completed machinery referred to in this document as ‘machinery’.
This document provides requirements and recommendations to prevent accidental and intentional (including
malicious) corruption of machines resulting in hazardous situations.
This document applies to:
—   hardware components, including interfaces to remote devices and control systems, that can transmit
signals or data;

—   software and data;

if they could influence the safety of the machinery.
NOTE 1     Topics can overlap with the domain of cybersecurity but are not necessarily identical in their coverage.

NOTE 2     This document does not describe functional safety requirements of control systems in machinery.

This document specifies requirements to related risks in all lifecycle steps.
Machinery interfaces to external systems and services are in the scope of this document. External systems and
services are out of the scope of this document.
This document does not apply to machinery installed before the date of its publication.
This document specifies requirements related to protection against corruption related risks in all lifecycle steps
such as:
—   development;

—   manufacturing;

—   commissioning;

—   operation;

—   maintenance;

—   decommissioning.

requirements of this document. For dated references, only the edition cited applies. For undated references, the
latest edition of the referenced document (including any amendments) applies.

title: (informative) Relationship between this European Standard and the essential

text: Either approach A (Clauses 5 and 7) or approach B (Clauses 6 and 8) shall be applied.
title: General

text:
The design and the construction of machinery shall not allow hazardous situations via connections.
A connection (physical, logical and indirect) is any link that can exchange information, for example:
—     a network link,

—     a WIFI connection,

—     a single wire,

—     wires of the power supply,

—     an optical link,

—     a card reader interface,

—     a connection from a machine to external systems:

— building networks

— cloud services

— service tools

NOTE 1       The connectivity can exist through equipment permanently available on site, or equipment temporarily brought
to the location during the installation, operation and maintenance, or decommissioning steps.

NOTE 2       Example of a machinery not to be considered is a simple drilling machine without any possibility of connection.
title: Connection of machinery

text:
Following a risk assessment according to EN ISO 12100:2010, where all potential hazards have previously
been identified, the designer shall perform a threat assessment.
The content of the threat assessment can be limited to additional threats that are not covered by the minimum
security measures.
The designer shall define the security context for the machine.
The following principles shall be applied in order to protect a machine from threats that can lead to hazardous
situation(s):
a)    Where vulnerabilities are present, eliminate those that can lead to hazardous situation(s).




      8

                                                                                                           prEN 50742:2025 (E)



EXAMPLE 1        To eliminate any unnecessary interfaces so that the threats cannot exploit this vulnerability.

EXAMPLE 2        JTAG interface(s) used during development and then disabled.

EXAMPLE 3        Elimination can be a result of redesign using different components (maybe from same vendor).

b)    if it is not possible to eliminate vulnerabilities, the designer shall mitigate them.

EXAMPLE          Mitigation, implementation of user authentication on an interface.

c)    For any vulnerabilities that remain after steps a) and b), information for use shall provide all necessary
information for compensating countermeasure by the user. See Annex C.

EXAMPLE            Manufacturer states in the instruction for use that the fieldbus connection of the machine is only designed
for internal(local) connections to another machine in a trusted network and is not allowed to be connected to an untrusted
network.

Vulnerabilities cannot create new hazards, but their exploitation can compromise the protective measures;
therefore, a threat assessment shall be performed.
NOTE       By exploitation of vulnerabilities via communication with the machine, the machine could be operated outside
safe parameters or degrade safety functions. The risk can only be assessed in terms of its impact on functional safety.

Countermeasures shall not negatively affect the functional safety of the machinery.
EXAMPLE           When a cryptographic function is implemented, it needs to be verified that it does not lead to hazardous
situations due to increased safety function response time.

The probability that someone will try to exploit a specific vulnerability for a malicious attempt cannot be predicted.
Therefore, the likelihood of being a target/victim shall not be relevant for the threat assessment.
In order to fulfil the essential requirements and recommendations to prevent accidental and intentional (including
malicious) corruption of machines resulting in hazardous situations, designers shall follow approach A in below
table.
However,   if   designers     prefer     to   follow   EN IEC 62443-3-3:2019,         EN IEC 62443-4-1:2018,
EN IEC 62443-4-2:2019 for the security requirements for their machinery, they shall follow approach B.

title: Introduction

title: Interfaces

text:
Security measures to protect against corruption of the machinery leading to hazardous situations shall be
selected on a risk-based approach in order to be adequate.
This risk-based approach shall consider both safety risks and threat risks of the machinery's intended use and
security context.
Security measures shall not negatively affect the functional safety.
title: General

text:
Where cryptographic methods are used, only state of the art algorithm should be selected.
NOTE 1    Information related to state-of-the-art algorithms is available from organizations such as ENISA
www.enisa.europa.eu. A list of examples is available in the bibliography [2][3][4].

NOTE 2      When a cryptographic function is implemented, it can be verified that it does not lead to hazardous situations
due to increased safety function response time.

title: Cryptography

text:
The following list provides types of interventions that shall be considered:
a.    safety parametrization/configuration parameters (via identification means like CRC…),

EXAMPLE connecting or disconnecting flash drive or SD card, when being used for storing configuration data and
logging data that is relevant for compliance of machinery

b.    SRESW update/modification (via identification means only, such as version number, CRC, ect…),

c.    SRASW updates/modification (via identification means only, such as version number, CRC, ect…),

d.    parametrization of human-machine interfaces if it can creates hazards,

e.    software relevant for displaying safety instructions.

NOTE 1      Any intervention that does not result in changes of the data listed above does not need to be logged (e.g.
successful/unsuccessful authorized interventions).

NOTE 2       Actions on the machine triggering a safe state of the machine e.g. triggering safety light curtain, are not in scope.

NOTE 3       The version of the SRASW binaries or SRESW binaries does not need to be kept in the tracing log.
title: Types of interventions

text:
Digital evidence of a legitimate or illegitimate action or event that changes or interrupts the behaviour, state or
operation of the machinery temporarily or permanently, that changes the software or data shall be recorded and
shall contain the following data as a minimum:
a.    an indication of the type of intervention that affects software relied on for risk reduction according to the risk
assessment,

b.    means to allow correlation of logged events, (e.g. timestamping referring to absolute or relative system
time), boot counts, system times, running counters,

c.    deletion of the log file.

NOTE         Timestamping can be provided by the device making the log event or the remote log collector.
title: Intervention evidence to be collected

text:
The machine shall provide digital or physical means for traceability related to interventions.
Digital evidence of interventions shall be readable and accessible.
The documentation shall provide information on how to access and interpret the recorded evidence.
If a binary format is used, the format should be documented as part of the information for use, so that anyone
can program a converter to make the logs intelligible.
Where collection of digital evidence is not reasonably practicable, physical evidence (e.g. tampering of a seal)
shall be used.
Evidence collection of interventions is required and shall be done automatically by the machinery or related
product.
NOTE         See Annex A for examples of recognized industry practice on logging standards.




      12

                                                                                                       prEN 50742:2025 (E)



The log records may be stored in the control system, the components inside the machine or in a component for
storing the data external to the machinery (e.g. Network Attached Storage (NAS), local hard drive, etc…).
title: Logging requirements

text:
Log storage shall contain, as a minimum, the evidence of the last intervention of each type.
Tracing log data records of each intervention shall be stored for at least five years.
The tracing log shall be enabled, as a minimum, from the time the machine is put into service.
title: Storage duration requirements

text:
Logs shall be properly secured to protect against tampering.
Log deletion, if applicable, shall only be possible by an authorized procedure.
title: Storage protection requirements

text:
Corruption can compromise the integrity and effectiveness of the risk-reduction measures, leading to potentially
hazardous consequences.
To safeguard against such risks, it is essential to first determine the required level of protection.
This involves identifying the vulnerabilities and specific needs of the application in question and defining Safety-
related Security levels (SRSL) for the individual risk-reduction measures.
Once the appropriate level of protection is identified, adequate measures can be applied to mitigate the threats
effectively.
These measures are intended to preserve the integrity and reliability of the safety control system.
title: General

text:
For each identified safety function, a Safety-related security level (SRSL) shall be determined and documented.
The determination of the SRSL shall be based on the result of the threat assessment and shall correlate to the
risk-reduction applied by the protective measure and to the likelihood of a successful threat exploitation.
Four SRSL levels are defined, where SRSL0 gives no specific additional requirements, and SRSL1 to SRSL3
correspond from low to high security levels.
NOTE       Annex B provides guidance for the determination of the SRSL. The likelihood of a successful threat exploitation
can be expressed as an attack potential (AP) being a function of several parameters such as Attacker Capability (AC),
Window of Opportunity (WoO) and Exposure Level (EL).

The measures associated with an appropriate Safety Related Security Level (SRSL) shall be selected to protect
safety functions.
Table 2 — SRSL description

       SRSL          Description
       SRSL0         This level shall be used for completely isolated safety system.
                     (e.g. completely isolated networks within the machine; or where safety functions have no
                     external interfaces.)
       SRSL1         This level (or higher) shall be selected to protect safety functions when the attack potential is
                     low, where an attack can only occur under very specific circumstances. When the severity of
                     the harm is reversible, it might also be selected for a moderate attack potential where an
                     attack has a reasonable likelihood of occurring.
       SRSL2         This level (or higher) shall be selected to protect safety functions when the attack potential is
                     moderate, where an attack has a reasonable likelihood of occurring. When the severity of the



                                                                                                                             13

      prEN 50742:2025 (E)




       SRSL          Description
                     harm is reversible, it might also be selected for a significant attack potential where an attack
                     has a high likelihood of occurring.
       SRSL3         This level (or higher) shall be selected to protect safety functions when the attack potential is
                     significant or critical, where an attack has a high likelihood of occurring or an attack is almost
                     guaranteed to occur.
                     This can be used for connection to untrusted networks e.g. connection to internet.
title: Safety-related Security levels

text:
The machinery shall meet, as a minimum, the security protection requirements listed below corresponding to
the determined SRSL.
The security protection requirements shall apply to their respective safety functions and their related interfaces.
NOTE        Interface can be “logical interfaces” (Modbus/TCP, Webserver….) on “physical interfaces” (RJ45, USB).
title: General

text:
SRSL0:
None.
SRSL1:
Entities shall be authenticated.
SRSL2:
Entities shall be authenticated.
SRSL3:
Entities shall be uniquely authenticated.
NOTE 1      In this context the word “entities” relates to human users, software processes, device capable of intervention.

NOTE 2      Authentication means include but are not limited to: passwords/ PIN/ dongle/ biometrics/ certificates/ RFID/
NFC/ logical identifiers (e.g. UID, HID, cookies, etc…) or via cryptographic authentication mechanisms such as random
challenge, TLS-handshake, X509 certificate, etc ….
title: Authentication

text:
SRSL0:
None.
SRSL1:
Interventions shall require authorization.
SRSL2:
Interventions shall require authorization.
SRSL3:
Interventions shall require authorization with specific privileges (e.g. role-based access control).




      14

title: Authorization enforcement

text:
SRSL0:
None.
SRSL1:
The integrity of software and other critical information such as safety-related configurations, shall be verified at
startup (e.g. by use of checksums).
SRSL2:
The integrity of software and other critical information, such as safety-related configurations, shall be verified at
startup and periodically (e.g. by use of checksums).
SRSL3:
The integrity of software and other critical information shall be cryptographically verified at startup and
periodically during operation (e.g. by use of cryptographic hashes, HMACs, CMACs).
title: Software and information integrity

text:
SRSL0:
None.
SRSL1:
Integrity of the boot process shall be protected and shall be verified at startup (e.g. checksums).
SRSL2:
Integrity of the boot process shall be protected and shall be verified at startup.
SRSL3:
A secure boot process shall be implemented (e.g. cryptographic signature verification with trusted roots, rollback
or safe state upon verification failure).
title: Integrity of boot process

text:
SRSL0:
None.
SRSL1:
The integrity of exchanged information shall be verified.
SRSL2:
The integrity of exchanged information shall be verified.
SRSL3:
The integrity of exchanged information shall be guaranteed by implementing secure cryptographic protocols
that detect and reject modified or replayed messages.
title: Information exchange integrity

text:
SRSL0:
None
SRSL1:
Input data shall be validated against defined boundaries.



                                                                                                                        15

      prEN 50742:2025 (E)



Invalid input data shall be rejected.
SRSL2:
Input data shall be validated rigorously, including syntax, semantics, format correctness, and data-type
verification.
Invalid input data shall be rejected.
SRSL3:
Input data shall be validated rigorously using strict, context-aware validation including syntactical, semantic,
boundary, and protocol-specific constraints.
Invalid input data shall be rejected.
title: Input data validation

text:
SRSL0:
None.
SRSL1:
Physical tampering shall be detected e.g. seal breaking.
SRSL2:
Physical tampering shall be detected e.g. seal breaking.
SRSL3:
Physical tampering shall be detected e.g. seal breaking.

text:
SRSL0:
None.
SRSL1:
None.
SRSL2:
The authenticity of critical data (e.g. SRESW/SRASW, and critical configuration data) shall be verified via e.g.
cryptographic signatures or equivalent at installation time.
SRSL3:
The authenticity of critical data (e.g. SRESW/SRASW, and critical configuration data) shall be verified via
cryptographic signatures or equivalent at installation time.

system and component requirements. This Clause defines the requirements for both machinery systems and
machinery components.

Examples of logging formats


This is an informative annex to provide the reader of the standard further information relating to logging formats.
It is however not necessary to follow these examples in order to meet the essential requirements outlined in this
document
CLF - Common Log Format: The Common Log Format is a file format that is used for logging web server
requests.
NOTE 1     See also RFC 6872; examples can be found here: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6872

Syslog: Syslog is a protocol for recording and transmitting log messages common on a wide range of systems.
Many types of network devices, IoT systems, desktops, and servers support the protocol and its standard
plaintext format makes messages easy for machines and humans to read.
NOTE 2     See also RFC 5424.

W3C extended Log File Format: the extended log file format is designed to meet the following needs:
—   permit control over the data recorded,

—   support needs of proxies, clients and servers in a common format,

—   provide robust handling of character escaping issues,

—   allow exchange of demographic data,

—   allow summary data to be expressed.

The log file format described permits customized logfiles to be recorded in a format readable by generic
analysis tools.

NOTE 3     Examples can be found here: https://www.w3.org/TR/WD-logfile

CEF - Common Event Format: The Common Event Format (CEF) is an industry standard format used in
conjunction with syslog messages by many security vendors to enable interoperability of events between
different platforms
The Common Event Format (CEF) is a standardized logging format developed by ArcSight (now part of Micro
Focus), a security information and event management (SIEM) solution provider. CEF is designed to simplify the
process of logging security-related events and making it easier to integrate logs from different sources into a
single system. CEF is based on the syslog format, which is a standard for message logging that is supported
by most network devices and operating systems.
BSI minimum standard for the logging and detection of cyber attacks: With this minimum standard, the BSI
defines a uniform approach to the detection of cyber attacks as required by the 2017 Implementation Plan while
establishing a basis for the specification and implementation of organizational and technical measures.

Threat assessment


To objectively determine the adequate and appropriate requirements, the first steps are to do define Assets,
Define Security Context, Trust Boundaries and model the system (e.g. by using a dataflow diagram), for example
as described in the relevant parts of Annex C.
The safety-related security level (SRSL) is the key property to decide on the appropriateness and adequacy of
protective measures. The level also determines which malicious attempts are reasonably foreseeable and must
be guarded against.
The first parameter to define is the Exposure Level (EL), which is proportionate to the attack surface of the
interface and connection under consideration.
An effective strategy to reduce the exposure level of safety functions is to perform network segregation between
safety relevant and non-safety relevant network parts.
All connections to safety functions need to be evaluated.
If a connection crosses Trust Boundaries (C.6), its exposure level is the higher one. E.G. a connection between
EL1 and EL2 will be considered as EL2.

gives the required safety-related security level to apply to the measure itself.

This example intents to show the effects on the threat model of an increased attack surface due to both a less
strict physical access control scheme and a more vulnerable wireless communication interface.
The loader crane is a crane mounted to a truck. It is typically used outdoors, and the crane part can be controlled
remotely

Cableless controlled loader cranes contain many sector specifics that are handled by respective standards. This
example will focus on two elements as the internal threats are already assessed in example 1:
—   The cableless controller connection according to EN 62745, consisting of

—   Controllers are treated as black box, threat model shall include only problems that can be introduced by

authenticate.

The security context depends on the intended use and application and includes, but is not limited to:
—    Protection of the perimeters of the security context, if applicable;

—    all countermeasures concerning the interaction between different functional units inside the security
context;

—    all countermeasures to be applied within the security context.

The countermeasures provided by security context are effective as long as assumptions of the following kind
are documented and fulfilled:
a)   physical and logical access management for the target users,

b)   intended use and foreseeable misuse.

c)   physical environment including compensating countermeasure,

d)   logical environment including compensating countermeasure,

e)   policies and procedures,

NOTE       “Security context” is the security equivalent of “intended use” in the safety domain.




      32

countermeasures provided by security context.
a)   physical and logical access management for the target users

— everybody

— authorized personnel

— service technician

b)   intended use and foreseeable misuse

— use remote diagnostic connection permanently to supervise

c)   Physical environment including compensating countermeasure

— location

— outdoors: agriculture, forest, construction sites, …

— public buildings, hospitals, schools …

— public transportation, airports, trains, …

— premises with access restrictions (access only allowed to people with a badge and authentication
etc.): Industrial facilities, logistic hubs, warehouses, …

— special restrictions

— locked cabinets

—    distinguish between locks with generic keys and unique keys.

— inside a machine’s housing

— physical position

— static

— mobile

d)   logical environment including compensating countermeasure

— allow only access via VPN?

— continuous connection or on demand only

— is some type of a firewall required if connected to a untrusted network?

— how is the network supposed to be installed (access to cables, communication partners, etc.)

text:
—    This machine is supposed to be used inside an industrial facility with standard access control, so only
authenticated and authorized personnel is allowed to near the machine.

—    The PLC is housed inside a locked cabinet with a unique key, which is handed to authorized personnel
only. (EL0 according to Annex B)

—    The network cables between motor drive and safety PLC are inside the machine and not accessible from
the outside without disassembling the machine. (EL0 according to Annex B)

—    Connection to the configuration interfaces is established only intermittently, only for service cases and
trouble shooting.

— For a direct connection (Ethernet or USB) between a PC and the PLC, EL1 can be assumed.

— The USB interface that allows for configuration of the PLC is connected to the edge of the cabinet
via a extension cable and thus can be accessed by people with physical access,
elevating the Exposure level from EL0 to EL1 according to Annex B

— The remote configuration connection is used only with a direct Ethernet cable or via a secured means
of remote access (e.g. a VPN)

— The secured remote access connection is left unpowered if no connection is needed (reducing the
“Window of Opportunity”)

— If remote access is desired, the Exposure Level might be for example EL4.

— Then the secured remote access connection needs to provide measures to reduce the risk from
EL4 with adequate measures as laid out in 5.4.

—    Connection to the standard PLC is kept up permanently for diagnosis and standard control activities

—    The memory device holding the safety configuration is placed inside the PLC inside the locked cabinet

text:
Trust Boundaries identify areas at a similar level of trust and isolate them from other areas at a different level of
trust. This applies to physical and logical properties. This is normally part of the data flow diagram, however it
can be considered a separate step as well.
The intention of grouping assets into zones and conduits is to identify those assets which share common security
requirements and to permit the identification of common security measures required to mitigate risk.
NOTE       The data flow diagram usually includes the trust boundaries of the system under consideration.




      38

                                                                                                  prEN 50742:2025 (E)




869

Figure C.9

NOTE

Boundary: edge

Zone: area inside a boundary

Practical examples consider, several different trust boundaries. Those trust boundaries correspond with the
different attack surfaces and can be labelled with the “Exposure Levels” defined in Annex B.
The examples show how to regard the system elements from the most trusted areas to the most exposed ones.
title: General

text:
This example considers everything inside the machine as a fully trusted environment, because it requires some
sort of authentication to access, e.g. a unique key or a special tool to open the machine, or some sort of software
authentication.
Components attached to the outside of the machine like a local HMI, the USB configuration interface of the
Safety PLC, and actuators are considered in the “physical access” category.
The Ethernet connection is intended to be used with local devices, such as fieldbus sensors and actuators or
other PLCs (thus “local access” exposure zone).
The industrial factory network contains access by engineering tools and other machines etc.
If the security context section in the information of use describes e.g. that the fieldbus connection is designed
to be used locally only, then compensating countermeasures are necessary to use the system in the intended
manner. This example mandates a network transition device (like a smart switch, a router with integrated firewall
etc.) to keep it separated from more exposure than allowed.
The same is true for other trust boundaries. As in our example the user shall be able to access the application
remotely, the remote access shall be secured by an external measure such as a firewall or a secure
communication end point to keep the adjacent level separated from the unrestricted level.

How can the interfaces or protocols be misused considering the defined assumptions?
You should use appropriate tools and techniques such as STRIDE for such a consideration.
Control system consists of INPUT – LOGIC – OUTPUT.
Our STRIDE analysis encompasses the whole system, including:
—    the control system consisting of INPUT – LOGIC – OUTPUT,

—    system interfaces,

Chain of trust concept: If data flows happen in a trusted boundary only, there
Spoofing – “impersonate a valid system user or resource” REF1 – violating authentication
—   Spoof another safety communication peer data, e.g. by faking stuffing scheme, time stamps, counters,
CRCs etc. between controllers, impersonating safety controllers

—   Replay attacks, simulating valid sensor data on a fieldbus

—   An attacker logs into a configuration interface as an administrator to modify safety configuration

Tampering – “Modifying system or user data” REF1 – violating integrity
—   Somebody modifies safety related parameters, configuration, firmware, or user software

—   Somebody performs a man-in-the-middle attack to modify process data while faking safety protocol’s
measures against communication errors

—   Somebody simulates/bypasses a safety input device, such as an E-Stop. The real E-Stop events are not
detected/evaluated correctly anymore.

Repudiation – “performing an illegal operation and denying involvement.”– violating accountability
—   Somebody deletes or modifies log entries related to modification of safety related parameters,
configuration, firmware, or user software

Information Disclosure – “expose information to individuals who are not supposed to see it” REF1 – violating
confidentiality
—   Probably not in scope as long as health and safety properties of the machine or related product remain
unchanged

Denial of Service – “Making the system temporarily unavailable or unusable” REF1 – violating availability
—   Probably not in scope as long as health and safety properties of the machine or related product remain
unchanged

Elevation of Privileges – “unprivileged user gains privileged access” REF1 – violating authorization
—   Probably not in scope as long as health and safety properties of the machine or related product remain

List of threats and mitigations

Threats should be countered primarily by countermeasures by this annex and if that is not practically reasonable,
compensating countermeasures should be considered.
Mitigations can either have an effect on
—    the impact of the attack,

—    or disrupt the attack path.

Goal should be a catalogue of possible mitigations, e.g.
—    input validation,

—    least privilege principle,

—    secure defaults,

—    kerckhoff principle, security should hinge on a well-defined secret, not on obscure design,

—    immutable application code,

—    separate memory for execution and data,

—    read-only memory,

—    etc.

Bonus if all of these mitigations get test criteria to make them verifiable.

Introduction
In today's increasingly interconnected world, the agricultural machinery, tractors, and earth-moving
machinery sector is becoming more reliant on technology and automation to improve efficiency,
productivity, and sustainability. Agricultural machinery, tractors, and earth-moving machinery have
evolved to incorporate advanced electronic systems, software, and communication technologies. These
advancements have brought about significant benefits, but they have also introduced new vulnerabilities
and risks associated with cybersecurity.
This document addresses the cybersecurity aspects in engineering of agricultural machinery, tractors, and
earth-moving machinery. By ensuring appropriate consideration of cybersecurity, this document aims to
enable the engineering of agricultural machinery, tractors, and earth-moving machinery to keep up with
state-of-the-art technology and evolving attack methods specific to the agricultural industry.
This document provides vocabulary, objectives, requirements, and guidelines related to cybersecurity
engineering.
ISO/IEC Guide 51 has been considered as far as practicable at the time of drafting of this document.
This standard is a Type C standard.

Agricultural machinery, tractors, and earth-moving
machinery – Product cybersecurity

1 Scope
This document defines process requirements for cybersecurity risk identification, risk handling, and
vulnerability handling for risks to the user. It addresses risks arising from cybersecurity threats, including
intentional malicious actions by external parties, while taking into account the operational environment
and assets requiring protection. These process requirements apply to the programmable electronic system
for a product (machine or component).
These process requirements apply during the product lifecycle (product development, production,
operations, and decommissioning phases).
These process requirements apply to remote data processing solutions only when they are essential to the
product’s functionality (e.g. remote precision farming). However, back-end services are beyond the scope of
this standard. For guidelines regarding back-end services, refer to enterprise solution standards.
This document additionally defines common language for communications about cybersecurity risks.
This document includes examples of cybersecurity damage scenarios, risk mitigation, and possible technical
solutions that are typical for the agricultural machinery, tractor, and earth-moving machinery industry.
This document includes activities that also apply to suppliers or third-party companies that are providing
the product or components for the end product.
This document applies to agricultural machinery, tractors, earth-moving machinery, construction
machinery, mining machinery, and forestry machinery.
NOTE      This document can also be used to assess the cybersecurity engineering requirements for other off-road
mobile machinery.

4 General considerations
The cybersecurity process described in this document is from the perspective of a product during all phases
of the product’s lifecycle to ensure an appropriate level of security.
A product consists of various components (e.g. the engine, wheels, and ECUs). Together all components are
used to fulfil the functions of a product (e.g. Driving and Remote Data Processing). In Figure 1, the product
(e.g. a tractor) consists of two functions (Function: Driving and Function: Remote Data Processing). The
Function: Driving contains the components wheel, engine, gearbox, Engine Control Unit and Transmission
Control Unit. The Function: Remote Data Processing contains the Telemetry Unit. The manufacturer (OEM)
defines the system of interest as shown in Figure 1 including the Engine Control Unit, Transmission Control
Unit, Telemetry Unit and messages between the ECUs.

Examples of cybersecurity relevant system of interest candidates:
— Safety related parts of a control system for use on agricultural and earth-moving machinery (e.g.[3] EN
  ISO 25119-1:2023 & A1:2023 or[4] EN ISO 19014-1:2018);
— Data related to operators or personnel, or to potentially sensitive information such as geolocation of
  machinery, field boundaries, or construction site layouts;
— Internal connections -- CAN (Controller Area Network), Ethernet, serial communication (e.g. RS-485), or
  TCP/IP for machine-to-machine communication;
— Interface to fleet management or telematics server; cellular or satellite telecommunications network,
  diagnostic interface;
— Wireless connected sensors or actuators – remote start/stop systems, RFID for operator authentication,
  or soil moisture sensors and load monitoring systems.
The cybersecurity process shall be applied throughout the supply chain to support the security engineering.
The security activities can be tailored to accommodate the needs of a specific situation. Manufacturer /
supplier for a specific system of interest agree on the responsibility-split for the applicable security activities.
The manufacturer may define roles that are accountable and responsible for the activities and work products
defined by the standard and to allocate those roles accordingly with sufficient resources and responsibility.

The system of interest shall have a risk assessment performed and risk treatments shall be identified
per clause 5. The risk assessment may be performed at different levels of a machine. For example, a risk
assessment may be done at the highest level of the machine considering the whole machine and external
interfaces. At a lower level, a risk assessment may be done on a sub-system of the machine such as steering
system, power train system, functional component, etc. For a product, all cybersecurity relevant sub-
systems shall be evaluated. Reference Annex A to understand the roles that should be included in a risk
assessment.

text:
Identify the assets and damage scenarios within the system of interest that may require cybersecurity
protection.
title: General
Prerequisites

text:
The damage scenario shall be identified. The list of damage scenarios should include:
— items such as, but not limited to, interrupting core product functions or essential services, stealing,
  manipulating, depriving, or deleting personal or other data / software; and
— at least the impact categories safety, financial, privacy, and availability for the user.
The manufacturer shall identify the asset(s) that can be the target of an attack to realize any identified
damage scenario.
Each identified asset shall be assigned one or more cybersecurity properties (e.g. confidentiality, integrity,
availability). Additional specific properties can be used (e.g. authorization, authenticity, non-repudiation,
freshness).
NOTE 1    A pre-defined list (e.g. damage scenarios, assets) can be created, maintained, and updated periodically by
the manufacturer.

NOTE 2    Asset list can include items such as:

—   Any data flow from an external connection interface that can be exploited to lead to a damage scenario;

—   Any commands, calibration, settings, configuration data which rest in the system of interest or is in transit to or
    from the system of interest that, if manipulated, can lead to a damage scenario;

—   Any personal data at rest or in transit to the system of interest;

—   Any hardware or software components related to core product functionality and safety of the system of interest.

The identification activity shall include the evaluation of accidental corruption that can lead to a damage

—   tampering;

—   data breaches;

—   denial of service;

—   misuse (implies intentional);

—   misconfiguration (implies unintentional).

title: Prerequisites

text:
The impact rating for each of the four impact categories (safety, financial, privacy, and availability) shall be
determined for each damage scenario using Table 1, Table 2, Table 3, and Table 4.
In the impact tables (Table 1, Table 2, Table 3, and Table 4), the assessor shall consider the users to be the
owner, operator, or bystander.
The maximum impact for each of the four impact categories (safety, financial, privacy, and availability) shall
be determined for the risk assessment. The categories with lower impact rating may be omitted.
EXAMPLE 1       Given the impact rating for the categories Safety: “Major”, Financial: “Moderate”, Privacy: “Negligible”,
Availability: “Negligible” will result in an overall rating of “Major”.

EXAMPLE 2       Given the impact rating for the categories Safety: “Negligible”, Financial: “Severe”, Privacy: “Negligible”,
Availability: “Negligible” will result in an overall rating of “Severe”.

Personal data can be defined in accordance with[9] ISO/IEC 29100:2024 for Table 3.

                                       Table 1 — Safety impact rating criteria
Impact Rating            Criteria for safety impact rating
Severe                   Life-threatening injuries (survival uncertain), severe disability
Major                    Severe and life-threatening injuries (survival probable), permanent partial loss in work capacity
Moderate                 Light and moderate injuries, requires medical attention, total recovery
Negligible               No injuries, damage limited to property
NOTE 1 This table aligns with definitions from[3] EN ISO 25119-1:2023 & A1:2023. Controllability and exposure in accordance
with[8] EN ISO 25119-2:2023 can also be considered for rating impact on safety, if a rational is provided.
NOTE 2 For earth-moving or construction machinery, the criteria descriptions of this table may be replaced by[4] ISO 19014-1:2018
criteria. Controllability and exposure in accordance with[4] ISO 19014-1:2018 can also be considered for rating impact on safety,
if a rational is provided.

Moderate                 Financial damage leads to inconvenient consequences which the affected user will be able to

Likelihood – Elapsed Time:
The elapsed time parameter includes the time to identify a vulnerability and to develop and successfully
apply an exploit. This parameter is measured in calendar time.
Likelihood – Specialist Expertise:
Specialist Expertise refers to the level of generic knowledge of the underlying principles, product type or

                                          Table 6 — Specialist Expertise
Layman:
Unknowledgeable compared to experts or proficient persons, with no relevant expertise.
EXAMPLE 1 Ordinary person using step-by-step descriptions of an attack that is publicly available.
Proficient:
Knowledgeable in that they are familiar with the security behaviour of the system of interest.
EXAMPLE 2 Experienced owner, ordinary technician knowing simple and popular attacks like odometer tuning, in-
stallation of counterfeit parts.
Expert:
Familiar with the underlying algorithms, protocols, hardware, structures, security behaviour, principles and concepts
of security employed, techniques and tools for the definition of new attacks, cryptography, classical attacks for the
product type, attack methods, etc. implemented in the system of interest.
EXAMPLE 3 Experienced technician or engineer.
Multiple experts:
Different fields of expertise are required at an expert level for distinct steps of an attack.
EXAMPLE 4 Multiple highly experienced engineers who have expertise in different fields (e.g. machine architecture,
communication protocols, feature control logic, software architecture), and which are required at an expert level
for distinct steps of an attack. Special Cybersecurity expertise includes for example state-of-the-art attacks such as
side-channels, cryptoanalysis, 0-day exploits.

Likelihood – Knowledge of System of Interest:
The knowledge of the system of interest is related to the amount of information the attacker is able to
acquire about the system.

                               Table 7 — Knowledge of the System of Interest
Public information:
Public information concerning the system of interest (e.g. as gained from the Internet).
EXAMPLE 1 Information and documents published on the product homepage or on an internet forum such as Open-
Source Documentation, industry standards, etc.
Restricted information:
Restricted information concerning the system of interest (e.g. knowledge that is controlled within the developer or-
ganization and shared with other organizations under a non-disclosure agreement).
EXAMPLE 2 Internal documentation shared between manufacturer and supplier, service documentation or software
update files that are restricted to service technicians, industry committee documentation.
Confidential information:
Confidential information about the system of interest, (e.g. knowledge that is shared between discrete teams within
the developer organization, access to which is constrained only to members of the specified teams).
EXAMPLE 3 Requirements and design specifications, software source code, security concept, risk assessment, custom
ECU designs, SBOM of proprietary components, AI training data.
Strictly confidential information:
Strictly confidential information about the system of interest (e.g. knowledge that is known by only a few individuals,
access to which is very tightly controlled on a strict need to know basis and individual undertaking).
EXAMPLE 4 Access to cryptographic keys, escalated access controls, credentials, passwords.

Likelihood – Window of Opportunity:
The window of opportunity parameter is related to the access conditions (e.g. time, type) to successfully
execute an attack. It combines access type (e.g. physical on the machine, logical by means of a simulator, and
remote via a network) and access duration (e.g. unlimited and limited). Depending on the type of attack this
includes discovery of possible targets, access to a target, time to perform attack on a target, ability to remain
undetected, ability to circumvent cybersecurity controls.

Unlimited:
High availability via public or untrusted network without any time limitation (i.e. asset is always accessible). Remote
access without physical presence or time limitation as well as unlimited physical access to the system of interest.
EXAMPLE 1 Remote attack (e.g. machine-to-anything or cellular interfaces) without any preconditions (e.g. authenti-
cation), unlimited physical access by the owner for chip tuning.
Easy:
High availability and limited access time. Remote access without physical presence to the system of interest.
EXAMPLE 2 Pairing time of Bluetooth, remote software update, remote attack that requires the machine standing still,
wireless infield communication.
Moderate:
Low availability of the system of interest. Either limited physical or logical access or both. Physical access to the product
interior or exterior without using any special tools.
EXAMPLE 3 Attacker enters an unlocked machine and got access to exposed physical interface (e.g. physical access
via on-board diagnostic port).
Difficult:
Very low availability of the system of interest. Impractical level of access to the system of interest to perform the attack.
EXAMPLE 4 Decapping an IC to extract information, cracking a cryptographic key by brute force faster than the key
is rotated.

Likelihood – Equipment:
Equipment refers to hardware, software or other equipment required to identify the vulnerability or execute
the attack.

                                                 Table 9 — Equipment
Standard:
Equipment is readily available to the attacker. This equipment can be a part of the product itself (e.g. a debugger in an
operating system) or can be readily obtained (e.g. internet sources, protocol analyser or simple attack scripts).
EXAMPLE 1 Laptop, CAN adapter, on-board diagnostic dongle, ordinary tools (e.g. screwdriver, soldering iron, pliers).
Specialized:
Equipment is not readily available to the attacker but can be acquired without undue effort. This can include purchase
of moderate amounts of equipment (e.g. power analysis tools, use of hundreds of PCs linked across the internet would
fall into this category), or development of more extensive attack scripts or programs. If clearly different test benches
consisting of specialized equipment are required for distinct steps of an attack this would be rated as bespoke.
EXAMPLE 2 Specialized hardware debugging device, manufacturer specific diagnostic software, machine on-board
communication devices (e.g. hardware in the loop test fixture, oscilloscope, signal generator), special chemicals.
Bespoke:
Equipment is specially produced (e.g. very sophisticated software) and not readily available to the public (e.g. black
market), or the equipment is so specialized that its distribution is controlled, possibly even restricted. Alternatively,
the equipment is very expensive.
EXAMPLE 3 Manufacturer-restricted tools, electron microscope.
Multiple bespoke:
Is introduced to allow for a situation, where different types of bespoke equipment are required for distinct steps of
an attack.

Likelihood Value = Elapsed Time Value + Specialist Expertise Value + Knowledge of System of Interest Value

6 Cybersecurity technical requirements for risk mitigation
title: Work products

text:
The purpose of this clause is to define technical requirements for mitigating cybersecurity risks. These
requirements establish the necessary security properties for ensuring the integrity, authenticity,
confidentiality, and availability of software and system components. Verification criteria are provided to
enable objective assessment and ensure proper implementation.
The manufacturer shall identify and document appropriate technical solutions that fulfil the specified
requirements (e.g. [WP-5.9-01]).
NOTE 1     The applicability of the technical requirements in this clause can be determined based on risk assessment
unless otherwise mentioned in the applicability clauses of clause 6.

NOTE 2    The term software in this document includes application software, firmware, boot code, etc.
title: Technical requirements introduction

text: Based on risk assessment.
title: Applicability

text:
Software security updates shall be made available to the product user.
The system of interest shall verify the authenticity and integrity of a software update.

The system of interest shall provide a method to determine the software version that is installed.
If automatic software updates are available, then the user shall be given the configuration option to opt out
of the automatic software updates.
If automatic software updates are available, then the user shall be given the ability to temporarily postpone
the automatic software update.
Where technically feasible, software updates to fix security issues shall be provided separate from functional
software updates.
title: Requirement

text:
This requirement ensures that the system of interest can quickly be securely updated in response to
vulnerabilities, minimizing the scalability risk throughout its lifecycle.
title: Rationale

text:
Ensuring the cybersecurity of system of interest involves implementing a secure and reliable update
mechanism. This clause outlines the best practices for designing such a function.
Before initiating any software update, it is important to authenticate servers delivering the updates. This
involves verifying the identity of these servers to confirm that updates are sourced from legitimate and
trusted entities.
The system of interest design should utilize digital signatures to guarantees the integrity and authenticity
of software images. Each update should be signed, and the system of interest should be equipped to verify
these signatures using public keys. This practice ensures that only trusted and untampered updates are
installed.
Incorporate a version control mechanism to prevent the installation of outdated or duplicate software
updates. This prevents regression to previous software versions that may have vulnerabilities.
Implement a rollback mechanism to manage update failures. This allows system of interest to revert to a
prior, stable version if an update does not complete successfully, ensuring minimal disruption to operations
and maintaining system stability.
Design the update function to support resumable downloads, allowing updates to continue seamlessly after
network interruptions. This capability can help in preventing incomplete installations due to connectivity issues.
title: Guidance

text:
Confirm the system of interest includes a mechanism to verify the authenticity and integrity of software
updates.
Verify the system of interest correctly executes a valid software update, where both the software and its
signature or other authenticator are valid.
Verify the installed software version is available from the system of interest.
Verify the system of interest detects and prevents the execution of an altered software update.
Verify the system of interest detects and prevents the execution of a software update with an invalid
signature or other authenticator.

title: Applicability

text: The manufacturer shall be able to notify the user that a security update is available.
title: Requirement

text: This requirement ensures that users are aware that an update is available.
title: Rationale

text:
Effective communication with users regarding software updates is important for maintaining the security
of machinery.
Notify users when new security updates are available, especially in cases where automatic updates have
been disabled or postponed (e.g. pop-up alerts, email notifications, or dashboard alerts).
Notification should include detailed information about the update's significance, highlighting its important
role in enhancing cybersecurity. Clearly communicate the potential impact on security and operational
performance if updates are delayed or ignored. By underscoring the importance, users are more likely to
understand the necessity of timely updates.
If updates are postponed, set recurring reminders or automatic reactivation of updates after the
postponement period expires.
title: Guidance

text: Confirm that a mechanism to notify users is in place when a security update is available.
title: Verification criteria
Secure software - integrity and authenticity check

text: Based on risk assessment.
title: Applicability

text:
The system of interest shall implement mechanisms to verify the integrity and authenticity of the software
components.
title: Requirement

text:
Ensure that the software that is executed on the system of interest has not been tampered and is from a
trusted source.
title: Rationale

text:
Those mechanisms can include, but are not limited to:
— Secure boot mechanism, an integrity check to protect machinery from unauthorized software execution;
— Periodical checks performed on the software integrity during runtime.
Those mechanisms usually rely on chain of trust models, for example a subsequent sequential verification
of the software components establishing a continuous trust chain, ensuring that only authorized and intact
software is executed. They make use of a security element as trust anchor such as HSM, or others (e.g. TPM,
cryptographic services engine, etc.).
Employ cryptographic algorithms and appropriate key lengths to ensure robust protection against
cryptographic attacks.

title: Applicability

text:
The system of interest shall be delivered in a secured state with development features disabled or secured
in production mode.
title: Requirement

text:
Production mode ensures that system of interest protection is enabled, and that no unnecessary, unprotected
capabilities are left open or available.
title: Rationale

text:
Hardening the design for the production release is important to minimize security risks, prevent
unauthorized access, and to limit attack surfaces. This hardening includes, but is not limited to, the following
measures:
— Disable or strongly protect development features such as test modes, and debug interfaces (e.g. protocols
  like XCP & SSH) before the final product is released to prevent unauthorized access or exposure of
  sensitive information. Examples of strong authentication includes cryptographic based authentication;
— Remove debug symbols, comments, and unreachable code from the production software to reduce the
  attack surface;
— Remove, disable or secure unused features, services, ports, or communication protocols that are not
  required for the final product, to reduce the attack surface;
— Confirm that cryptographic artifacts, such as production keys and certificates, are securely generated,
  injected, and protected according to security requirements.
title: Guidance

text:
Confirm that debug symbols, comments, and unreachable code are removed from the production software.
Verify that development features and interfaces are either disabled or strongly secured in production mode.

text: Ensures specific risk-related events are detected.
title: Rationale

text:
Ensuring continuous monitoring and detection of unexpected or abnormal behaviours enhances the security
of the system of interest and helps identify potential threats. This includes, but is not limited to:
— Monitoring and logging abnormal resource usage patterns, like sudden spikes in CPU, memory, or
  network usage, that can signal a potential security incident;
— Capturing security event details, including timestamps, identities (e.g. user, component), event types (e.g.
  resource spike, abnormal operation), occurrence counts, and results (e.g. success, failure) if applicable;
— Adding anomaly detection rules based on the system of interest’s operational context, considering
  factors like operational mode and diagnostic modes (e.g. a machine behaving erratically outside normal
  operating hours).

text:

failed digital signature checks, failed secure boot processes, failed message authentication checks.
title: Requirement

text:
Detecting and logging integrity violations enhances security and helps identify potential tampering. This
includes, but is not limited to:

  signature verification during secure updates, failed secure boot processes, or detection of unauthorized

— Logging violations related to data and message integrity, such as failed message authentication checks,

that these cover relevant integrity violation scenarios.

title: Verification criteria

text: Based on risk assessment.
title: Applicability

text:
The system of interest shall implement multiple layered security mechanisms to reduce the impact of
cybersecurity incidents, following a defence in depth approach.
title: Requirement

text:
A defence in depth approach uses multiple, redundant, diverse layers to ensure that if one layer fails,
subsequent layers will mitigate the risk, enhancing overall resilience against threats.
title: Rationale

text:
The defence in depth layered strategy increases the system’s resilience by reducing the likelihood that a
single vulnerability or failure will lead to compromise or major impact.
Each layer needs to be designed with independence in mind, so that the compromise of one does not
invalidate others and with the target to limit the actions of an attacker. Defence in depth is not only about
redundancy, but also diversity in controls and strategies, addressing both technical and operational aspects
of system security.
Defence in depth can include, but is not limited to:
— Implementing preventive measures to reduce the attack surface and block threats before they materialize
  (e.g. access controls, segmentation, cryptography);
— Implementing detection mechanisms to identify ongoing or attempted attacks (e.g. access monitoring,
  anomaly detection, intrusion detection systems);
— Implementing resilience and recovery mechanisms to maintain or restore functionality in the event of an
  incident (e.g. protection, recovery, and secure update mechanisms to mitigate impacts of incidents).
title: Guidance

text:
Confirm that the system of interest has been designed with consideration for a defence in depth strategy,
including the use of multiple, independent, and diverse security mechanisms to mitigate cybersecurity risks.
title: Verification criteria

text:
This requirement applies wherever cryptographic mechanisms are used to fulfil other cybersecurity
requirements (e.g. for ensuring confidentiality, integrity, authentication, or secure updates).

title: Requirement

text:
The effectiveness of cryptography relies on the use of standardized and widely accepted algorithms that
have been peer-reviewed and validated. Following cryptographic best practices, including the application of
recommended key lengths, reduces the risk of vulnerabilities and helps maintain resilience against evolving
threats.

7 Product Lifecycle
title: Verification criteria

text:
Product cybersecurity is central in all phases of the product lifecycle to ensure the security and integrity of
the product, its data, and its users. Below are the phases of the product lifecycle along with details on how
cybersecurity should be addressed.
title: Rational

text:
The manufacturer shall perform a risk assessment per clause 5, create a risk report [WP-5.8-01], and create
a cybersecurity requirements specification [WP-5.9-01] during the design phase per clauses 5.8 and 5.9.
If the design changes during development, then the risk assessment, risk report [WP-5.8-01] and
cybersecurity requirements specification [WP-5.9-01] shall be updated if necessary for the system of
interest that changed.
title: Design phase

text:
Implement the cybersecurity requirements specification [WP-5.9-01] defined in the design phase.
During the implementation phase, the manufacturer should ensure that all software development activities
comply with the manufacturer’s secure coding guidelines. The coding guidelines can be referenced by the
cybersecurity requirements specification.
title: Implementation phase

text:
Functional testing shall be performed to verify that the cybersecurity requirements specification [WP-5.9-
01] security measures have been implemented.
The verification criteria shall include the defined verification methods from clause 6 for the selected
technical solutions.

                                                              ﻿
                                             © ISO 2025 – All rights reserved
                                                            37

                                Licensed to Inlab / Simone Fornaciari (s.fornaciari@inlab.srl)
                             ISO Store Order: OP-1037245 license #1/ Downloaded: 2026-03-26
                                Single user licence only, copying and networking prohibited.
                                           ISO/DIS 24882:2025(en)

The verification of the implementation may be achieved using different functional testing methods.
The following are examples of such functional testing methods:
— Static code analysis;
— Fuzz testing;
— Unit testing;
— Code reviews.
Testing may be documented in the form of a test procedure. A test procedure can include but is not limited to:
— Objective definition (what should be achieved with the test);
— Test methodology (what kind of tests should be carried out);
— Acceptance criteria (what conditions must be met for the test to be considered passed);
— Test protocols (schemes for documenting the test results).
A verification test report [WP-7.2-01] shall be created to document the results of the testing.
title: Verification phase

text:
In the validation phase, the manufacturer shall review the overall product to confirm that the risk assessment
and security goals were met.
For products that include off-the-shelf and open-source components, the overall product validation may
include work products [WP-7.2-02] and [WP-7.2-03] related to clauses 9.3 and 9.4.
The manufacturer shall create a validation report [WP-7.2-02] to document the results of the validation review.
The validation and verification reports may be combined in a single document.
Additional testing can be performed to evaluate the effectiveness of the product security such as penetration
testing, fuzz testing, etc. This testing can help to identify threats that were not considered during the
risk assessment. If new threats are identified, then the risk assessment, risk report [WP-5.8-01], and
cybersecurity requirements specification [WP-5.9-01] shall be updated to include the new threats.
title: Validation phase

text:
The manufacturer shall perform a conformity assessment to make sure all processes were performed
correctly, and the requirements derived in the risk assessment were addressed.
The manufacturer shall create a conformity assessment report [WP-7.2-03] to document the assessment
results.
title: Conformity assessment phase

text:
The production phase is the period while the product is in the manufacturing facility.
The manufacturer shall support production steps that are required to realize the security features of
the product (e.g. enable security by default configuration, injecting of certificates, disable development
interfaces, reference production mode in clause 6.6).
The manufacturer shall install the latest released product software including any security updates that are
available.
